articles.title: THE GLAD TIDINGS AND THE LORD’S SUPPER
articles.author: J. N. Grace
articles.meeting: Word in meeting for ministry, Melbourne

paragraphs.text: We have been speaking of the days in which we are, the last days, and in fact the last hour.

Our hymn referred to the Lord and how we are looking for His coming in a little while. I was thinking of these chapters which relate the last hours of Jesus, and that there must be some correspondence between the last hours of our Lord, and the last days of the assembly’s history. It is well for us to think over that as to what our expectations might be. We are not in the pristine days of the church’s history; we are in days of brokenness, in days of complete public failure; we have humbly to say that. But in acknowledging that, we have the understanding that the Lord has not changed, the Spirit has not changed, and the truth has not changed. We can go forward in the faith of our souls that the dispensation is going to end just as the Lord intended. The Spirit’s work will be as complete as the work of Christ and that completion, of course, may take place in a very short time, think the final touches of the Spirit’s work will be very short as regards the period of time, but what a work it will be in the way of quality!

So I was thinking of these two outstanding things connected with the last period of the Lord’s life when He had His own with Him in Bethany. One refers to the glad tidings and the other refers to the Lord’s supper. If we can lay hold of these two things as being what the enemy has attacked, but what the Lord will sustain, I think we will

continue to commit ourselves fully to them. We may set ourselves in our minds, beloved brethren, to the fact that the last days of the church’s history will be a time of stress, difficult times, times of sorrow. I think we are all aware of how much sorrow there is in the histories of individuals, in our own history, in the history of local companies, and in the history of what there is universally, what sorrow has entered into it.

In Matthew 26 the passover is about to take place, against a murderous background. The whole official line of things that professed to hold what was of God had gathered together in counsel against Jesus that they might kill Him. That is a very sorrowful condition of things; the Person of Christ was among them and they wanted to kill Him. He had no place in that world, and He has no place in the world now; the world does not want Jesus. They will have the outward trappings of christianity, they will have all that will minister to the glory of man, but the Person of Christ is not wanted.

But there was one woman who wanted Him and she was prepared to go forward in the face of hostility, into an atmosphere which was against her, with one object in her heart, and that was to make much of Christ. It does not say she was invited into Simon’s house, but she came there and she was not afraid of the indignation of the disciples, those who should really have appreciated everything she did. There was indignation when someone came in to make much of Christ! Think of that! This woman braved it all; what a sister she was! Come what may she was not going to turn aside from what was in her heart, which was to make much of Jesus, to make everything of Him. She had this alabaster flask of very precious ointment that had been saved up; it was costly; what it had cost her! What it costs so many today as we think of many prepared
to move forward in the face of sorrow, suffering, and hostility to make everything of Christ.

He says, “Ye have the poor always with you, but me ye have not always”. It is as if the Lord says that this kind of person is an exemplification of the glad tidings. I would like to be like this woman to whom the Lord called attention. We can preach, maybe; we can speak; but are our lives really a testimony to the fact that we love Jesus, and that, beyond all else, He means everything to us?
Well, that is what this woman meant; she poured out this ointment; there were no reserves.

How often we have reserves. The Lord had no reserves in relation to us; He has given His life, has He not? He has given His all. Well, this woman gave her all. The Lord says, “In pouring out this ointment on my body, she has done it for my burying”. She saw the way out that the Lord was taking, the way through death, beloved, and He has been that way for us.

He then says, “Wheresoever these glad tidings may be preached in the whole world, that also which this woman has done shall be spoken of for a memorial of her”. That is the value of this service in the sight of heaven, the value of an action that made much of Christ. This woman was an outstanding exemplification of the result of the glad tidings.

Along with the glad tidings there is the Supper. It is not only what we are in testimony in relation to the glad tidings. The Supper is not something we have instituted; it is something the Lord has prepared and given to us. In this gospel He says in effect. This kind of woman has to be sustained; this kind of testimony has to go through, and I will provide in the Supper just what is needed, the food and the drink; it will enable you to be maintained in the scene of testimony until I come. That is Matthew’s presentation of
the Supper; it is not the memorial exactly, which is Luke; Matthew gives us food and drink.

How considerate of the Lord, is it not, that He has taken account of us in a hostile scene, where everything is against us because everything is against Himself, and has provided exactly what is needed in this, the end of the dispensation, that we should be maintained in testimony in the face of all the opposition that the enemy can bring to bear.
We may have to go on just in smallness of numbers because in the decline of things others have given up the truth, but the Lord says in the Supper, I have provided just what you need.

“This is my body”. He says, an allusion to the way the Lord has carried out the will of God, and every time we partake of the Supper it just means that as we put our hand to the loaf we say to the Lord, ‘Well, Lord, we want to do the will of God too’. Then we drink of the cup, and as you drink something enters into you to strengthen your heart, and to stimulate and refresh you. A fresh sense of the love of God coming in in the giving of Jesus, and His own love expressed in the shedding of His blood; how wonderful it is! He says, “For this is my blood, that of the new covenant, that shed for many for remission of sins”. How liberating it is! It is no system of bondage, but your heart is liberated as you think of this. You think of others around you; He says, “shed for many for remission of sins”, and even if it is only a few of us gathered together to partake of the Supper, all the saints are in our hearts. It belongs to all, it really does; all God’s thoughts are available for them; He has in His mind that what is established in Christ is for all who will take advantage of it.
Oh I think that one of the results of the discipline and the sorrows that we have been through

is that our hearts have been enlarged in relation to the thoughts of God. We have been too narrowed up in our thoughts and affections; we have still to be narrowed up as to our feet, but we can go out in our affections when we think of the basis of everything being in the death of Jesus, and the love of God expressed in the shedding of the blood of Jesus, and our hearts can embrace all our brethren. You may say, ‘Well, is that so?’ The Lord says, “shed for many”; can you tell me just how many? I cannot tell you how many, but I hang on to that word

“many”. In the light of it your heart goes out to all your brethren. How many there are who need to be recovered to the truth; how many there are to be salvaged from all that the enemy has done, and if they were all recovered we would still think there are others to be gained through the gospel to come into the enjoyment of what has come to us by way of the shed blood of Jesus.

So our hearts can be assured, stimulated, and strengthened to know that in the covenant, in what God has done in the blood of Jesus. He has committed Himself to us and He is never going to go back on it. Do we trust Him? Do we think that because publicly everything has gone down—publicly the whole thing has broken up—God is not going to see us through?

We stand by the truth, and God will give us the persons. We not only know that as something that has been said to us, but we can prove it. So let us stand by the truth and enjoy what God has brought within our range, and be like this woman who poured out this ointment, poured it out, the Lord said that; there were no reserves with her. Well, let there be no reserves with us, dear brethren, but full committal to the testimony of our Lord.

articles.title: “ASK WHAT I SHALL DO FOR THEE”
articles.author: W. Dickson

paragraphs.text: We have been conversing together over great things, heavenly things, but it is a comfort to know that the greatest things in christianity are open to desire. This immediately opens the prospect for everyone in this room. No one need say, ‘If I had greater mental capacity’, or ‘If I had greater physical energy, or a better environment, I would be able to touch these things’.

The greatest thoughts of God, on the unqualified testimony of Scripture and in the experience of countless saints, the greatest things in christianity are open to desire. I have read these scriptures to speak simply about them. In each case persons were asked the question as to what they would desire. What would you desire, beloved brethren? I trust our appetites have been whetted during these days, whetted for heavenly things. Perhaps we have been negligent. How that word comes home to all of us, comes home to me as I stand here. How often I have neglected the opportunity of acquiring heavenly things. But tonight the Spirit of God would say, “Ask what I shall do for thee”.

This young man Elisha had accompanied Elijah. It is interesting to note the places to which Elijah goes with Elisha. He covers in his movements the whole testimonial sphere. It is remarkable that Elijah did not take him to Jerusalem. He took him to Gilgal, Bethel, Jericho, and the Jordan, but he did not take him to Jerusalem. He took Elisha back over the whole
testimonial area, and said to him in effect, ‘I am leaving the scene of my labours to you.

Elisha, to see whether you can be a workman approved of God’. Elisha went round that testimonial area and when Elijah said to him, “Ask what I shall do for thee, before I am taken away”. Elisha said to him, “I pray thee, let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me”. It would appear to me that as Elisha surveyed the extent of the testimonial position and what had to be carried in heavenly power, he recognised that it called for a double portion of the Spirit. And, beloved brethren, it does call for a double portion of the Spirit.

Elijah said, “Thou hast asked a hard thing”. Why should it be a hard thing for this request to be granted? Well, I think it is only when you see Christ up there in glory that you will feel yourself equipped in a double portion of the Spirit to cover the testimonial sphere. ‘If you see me when I go up’, Elijah said. Have you seen Him go up? Do you know only the Christ of the gospels? Is your knowledge of that blessed Man limited (I speak reverently) to what came out here in Him as Man? or do you know Him as having gone up there to glory, having smitten the waters of Jordan?—Elijah “took his mantle, and wrapped it together, and smote the waters”. Why did he wrap it together? Beloved brethren, when Jesus went into death there was in that blessed Man the concentrated power of God able to deal with every adverse power and influence that would range itself against the testimony. That was the Person that Stephen saw at the right hand of God, standing there to sustain His servant in the hour when he was passing over Jordan.
Beloved brethren, have we all a double portion of the Spirit? In my application of the scripture at this time the double portion of the Spirit lies in this, that one portion is the Spirit given to

you on the principle of gift, and the other portion is the Spirit given to you on the line of desire. There are many believers in this world who have in that sense only one portion of the Spirit. They have the Spirit on the line of gift. But power in the testimonial position lies in the Spirit asked for as power, a double portion. As we have our eyes fixed on Christ in glory we are equipped for the heavenly road and every exigency of the testimonial position here.

In the passage in Joshua 15 the question was asked, “What wouldest thou?” Caleb had issued a challenge as to the overthrow of Kirjath-sepher, and Othniel had come on to view and taken the city and got Achsah, Caleb’s daughter, as wife. Have we all got Achsah? Kirjath-sepher,
‘the city of the book’, is the mind of man entrenched against God, and was overthrown in Paul’s ministry—Acts 19 shows us the smiting of Kirjath-sepher. But have we got Achsah?
In other words, is the truth of the assembly worked out subjectively with us? Do we hold the truth of the assembly merely objectively, or have we Achsah as wife? That is the challenge.

You will have her when you take on subjectively the truth of what Paul did in his ministry when he overthrew this stronghold of Satanic power to establish this great and wonderful thought of the assembly for Christ and for God.

“It came to pass as she came, that she urged him to ask of her father a field”. May I be practical? There are a lot of young people here today. Do you urge your husband to ask, for a field? Do you urge him to go in for spiritual things? Do you urge him not to allow work or hobbies, or other things of this life, to hinder him in that field? Whatever you do, get that field, so that you can cultivate it for the inheritance of God, for the service of God, and
bring forth fruit from the field. Caleb said, “What wouldest thou?”, but first of all it says,

“she sprang down from the ass”. Beloved brethren, you will not get spiritual things of any substance unless you spring down from the ass. I would like to give you an illustration from real life. Some years ago an old brother visited one whom the Lord appeared to be using and helping, and found him with a mountain of books around him, deep in study. The old brother said, ‘You know, so-and-so, that is not the way to get it’. The brother said, ‘How would you get it?’ The old brother indicated his knees! That is how we spring off the ass, to abandon human support, human resources, and learn something of the power of prayer in regard to the entrance into the heavenly things that God has in His heart.

She said, “Give me a blessing; for thou hast given me a southern land; give me also springs of water. Then he gave her the upper springs and the lower springs”. A double portion of the Spirit!—the upper springs—the power to enter into the great realm of privilege, and the lower springs, the power to testify here in heavenly freshness. “Springs”, the scripture says, not ‘the upper brook and the lower brook’; “the upper springs and the lower springs”—power, heavenly vitality, the double portion of the Spirit. Have we asked for a double portion of the Spirit? Have we asked for the upper springs and the lower springs? Beloved brethren, may we get the gain of the Holy Spirit as the power to enter into heavenly things and to sustain us here in testimony in the heavenly path, for His name’s sake.

I want to speak a little, dear brethren, about the matters of deliverance and escape which come into these scriptures I have read, and also the way in which every experience that we have is intended to enrich the divine system. Not of course that this system is in need of enrichment in one way since it is ample and sufficient in itself. But as in the sphere of testimony, our experiences with God are intended to help us to contribute to it by way of thanksgiving and praise and thus to glorify God. It would not be difficult to see the distinction between deliverance and escape; the one is what is done for us, the other is what we do for ourselves.

We will first notice verse 14 of the psalm which gives us a link with the previous meeting as to what is for God. The writer says, “Offer unto God thanksgiving”. He would look for this by way of sacrifice. It is to be the first thing with us to do this, and not only for temporal things and mercies. We can give thanks that we have been brought up in a christian household where the testimony is valued, for having the Scriptures, and for the various blessings that we have. The apostle wrote to the Ephesians of God, “who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenlies in Christ” (Ephesians l: 3). Not just all blessing, but every distinct blessing. Thus we can perform our vows to the Most High. Let us remind ourselves, and the young people especially, that God sets great store upon absolute committal

to Him and His interests. He will see to it that there is all that is needed in the testimony, for He is the Most High, known to us in this way as well as others (see Acts 7: 48). We are to perform our vows to Him. It is not that we make a certain vow and are upset if we are not able to keep it, or congratulate ourselves if we do keep it. What is meant is rather devotedness at all costs of the heart to the interests of God in this scene, and He sets great value on it.

Then it says, “Call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver thee”. It might not be actual crises in outward things that this would point to, but rather I think to what we call soul experience. The young people need to take the things of life in a more purposeful way, recognising that the Lord is dealing with them. He allows circumstances, words of ministry, happenings in the household, blessings and favours from heaven, to come to them that they may be in exercise in their souls towards Him. Evidently there is in the psalmist’s mind great scope for deliverance and as a consequence that “Thou shalt glorify me”.

If you were able to take a royal letter and liberate righteously someone in prison, would not that be a fine thing? That person would be set free by the truth. But supposing the Queen were to send the Prince of Wales personally, that person would be set free by the son. It shows the distinction, that God would not only have the believer absolutely set free by the truth, but to know it as a personal matter between himself and the Lord. The man in John 9

was set free by the truth when he arrived at knowing one thing, that he was blind before whereas now he saw. But it was when the Lord Jesus found him outside and spoke to him that he was really set free by the Son. He was able to worship Him and bring his tribute, so
that it is not merely a matter of deliverance as a doctrine but of knowing the Deliverer Himself, “Jesus, our deliverer”, 1 Thessalonians 1: 10.
There are three men mentioned in Ezekiel 14 in connection with the matter of deliverance.

Noah, Daniel, and Job. They would not have been able to free anyone else, but they knew what freedom was themselves. Noah, particularly, knew deliverance from judgment. If there is anyone here who is unconverted, you need to know what this is. All around Noah was judgment. We need constantly to be aware that God has saved the believer by a salvation which should insulate us entirely from the world-system that is under judgment, though we have to do with it. A young man in London told us once that he wished to go out of fellowship so as to have a wider path. We went to see him and told him that he made us think of someone in the ark who wished to be thrown out for a swim. You cannot think what the consequences of it would be. Well, such is the world around us morally as under condemnation. You may say that it goes on much as it always did. That may appear so, but it is under judgment nevertheless. It is in His longsuffering and mercy that God has not yet brought in the judgment in actual fact. He is not willing that any should perish.

Then you would need deliverance from Satan’s present power as well. There were those in bondage in Egypt even though they were under shelter of the blood from judgment. They were not free from Pharaoh’s power until they went through the Red Sea with walls of water on either side of them. The bearing of the death of Jesus on your behalf delivers entirely from the known power of Satan and of sin. Looking back, the Israelites minimised what that deliverance was, they tended to forget, and we are often like that. We have to have refresher courses in these matters, hence the ministry given to us often dwells on these elementary and basic matters in order that we might deepen in the intensity of soul experience. What our deliverance has meant for Jesus! The Israelites, though in fear, went through the Red Sea in perfect order by faith. It is the only thing said of them that they did, as a whole, by faith. Thank God for giving us faith that we may enjoy deliverance from sin and from Satan’s power—it is through seeing that in Christ having died we have died as well. As to deliverance from law, anyone who has put himself under it will know how it leads to disappointment. It leads to the cry in Romans 7—“Who shall deliver me out of this body of death?” (Romans 7: 24), but then there is the tribute—“I thank God, through Jesus Christ our Lord” (verse 25).

Then there is deliverance from the world system. Daniel could say much about this in its various forms. By purpose of heart he became free of the whole system of unholy culture that was built up in Babylon where his lot was cast. He would not take the food of idolatry that was offered to him. I feel, dear brethren, that we all need to set our hearts more in the true direction, as it were to have our compass thoroughly adjusted and sail according to it. Then Daniel was delivered from the world of difficulties by prayer. When the question came that all the wise men had to be slain (Daniel 2: 13), he and his companions would suffer as well.

That was a solemn trial to be in! But he called upon the prayers of his companions that God would be merciful and show him Nebuchadnezzar’s dream in order that not only their own lives might be preserved but also those of others. How good God is that if we know deliverance we can be a help to others.

Then there was the furnace. I know that it was the three companions there, but they followed the same principle in that they yielded themselves to God and their bodies a living sacrifice and were freed from the whole world of fear. I feel very much the bearing of fear upon us in the testimony. Even amongst ourselves we have known what it has been as a power working against peace and restfulness. God’s thought is that we should be delivered by being devoted entirely to Him, having placed our bodies on the altar. Later, Daniel was freed from the world of ambition as well. When there was the opportunity of his being loaded with benefits by Belshazzar, he said in effect, ‘Let the gifts be to another, but I will read the writing’. He was ready to be of service, but was not caught in the snare of ambition.

Then Job had to know what it was to be delivered from self. He was a man to whom God was looking for His tribute, but he delayed payment. He is an example of one who in the end glorified God but first had to be set free from self—not the bad self so much as the ‘good’

self. God was working with him. He was empowered by God to maintain his integrity all through, but had to come to an end of self. It says that “Jehovah accepted Job” (Job 42: 9) when the burnt offerings were made and he prayed for his friends.
Well, deliverance is one side of the truth, the other is to make our escape. Peter speaks of

“having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust”. This epistle from which we have read is especially interesting. It is not written to any individual or class of persons, excepting that it is to “them that have received like precious faith” with the apostle and others. You can put yourself in there, for you have received precious faith. Thank God for that; and you have
received it through the righteousness of God, so that it can never be taken away. God has a direct word for you as if you had received this letter in the post, a message of great importance.

Now I suppose that one danger in escaping is that you might get caught again. Once you are delivered from a thing, though you may become hazy as to the doctrine or the enjoyment of it, yet as a thing accomplished for you it can never be changed because God has done it for you; “Jesus, our deliverer”, 1 Thessalonians 1: 10. But escaping has its own exercises because you might be entangled with the same things again. The apostle warns of that (2

Peter 2: 22). But to escape shows that you have a horror of being detained in any evil that you might be in, and one great way is to flee. You have power to do this. “Youthful lusts flee”, the apostle says in 2 Timothy 2: 22. That is not only things that persons with natural conscience speak of as evil or wicked, but would extend to desiring things that are not in God’s mind for us. We are to flee from those, but there is the power of attraction as well as that of compulsion. You are not only fleeing from something but have something of God to which to escape—“Pursue righteousness, faith, love, peace, with those that call upon the Lord out of a pure heart”. Thank God that there are those that are calling on the Lord, not only on His name but on Him personally, with whom we can follow these things.

We read of people who escape by going underground. The believer is able to do that too. In fact that is what baptism is—going under water in actual fact. The understanding of it is really that you go out of sight by being baptised to Another, even Christ Jesus. It says of the Israelites that they “were baptised unto Moses in the cloud and in the sea”, 1 Corinthians 10: 2. The cloud comes first there. The blessing set before them was one thing, but they were baptised in the sea as well, so that they really escaped from Egypt by being identified with Moses. Now the Lord Jesus has been buried, and His burial was on behalf of each one of us, so that for one thing we make our escape from the world system by going out of sight. Paul, you remember, says that he escaped from one who would have laid hands on him. He was let down in a basket, which some say was the kind of thing in which the dead bodies were taken out of the city (see 2 Corinthians 11: 33). No doubt he was gently let down by the brethren but nevertheless there was the humiliating side of it. So it was by accepting death really that he escaped the hands of one who would have bound him. Do not let us ignore the fact that there is an enemy, not only of our souls personally, but of the whole testimony of God here, who is concerned to capture us. It is not that we have to die to sin, but we have to reckon ourselves already dead to it and maintain the reckoning and so keep our freedom.

I mentioned that by our experiences we are enabled to enrich the whole divine system. What I mean by the divine system here is that, as in the world there are forms of government, so in God’s world there is government, not a democracy but a real kingdom, so different morally from the world’s systems. And God’s government is a very real thing which works always for good for those who desire good, but is against those who work evil. The principle of it can be seen in the fact that if we sow to the flesh we reap corruption (see Galatians 6: 8). If we sow to the Spirit we reap a crop to eternal life, making it attractive to us and enriching the system.

Then, just as the world has welfare systems, we find that God has one. We have read about it in the Epistle of Peter—“His divine power has given to us all things which relate to life and godliness”. If that is not a welfare system I do not know what is! It does not cost us anything but is provided freely in order that believers might in their turn support God’s interests here.

He has a commercial system as well. According to the parable, when the high-born man went away he gave to his own bondmen some money and said, “Trade while I am coming”. Luke 19: 13. You will remember that the bondmen came to their lord and brought their gains with them, saying for instance, “Thy mina has produced ten minas”. In other words, they were not just taking the benefit of their exchange and commerce to themselves, but they were enriching their lord’s possession. We engage in trade, I suppose, by conversation with one another and in reading meetings. Indeed all our gatherings have an element of the trading floor, where there is exchange and profit. As has often been said, if one exchanges impressions of Christ with another believer both are doubly well off. And so it goes on, and the progression increases so that there is a great enrichment.

There is one great difference between the world’s sphere and God’s. The world has an entertainment system, which God does not have. What he has in its place is one of joy, which is far greater. We do not come to meetings to be entertained but that we might rejoice together in the things that God has given us. We bring the whole tithe into the treasury in order that we might know the heavens opened and a blessing poured out upon us (see Malachi 3: 10).

There is a further way, dear brethren, in which we can cause enrichment. We were reading elsewhere about the trees in Jotham’s parable (see Judges 9). They contributed to the divine system by just being what they were where they were. The olive-tree would bear its fatness, and do just what it was intended to do. The fig-tree would produce its sweetness and the vine its wine. They benefited “God and man”. It shows that the divine system really includes man—God and man together. I think that it is a wonderful thing to think of. Not only is there a tribute going up to God, and a blessing coming down from Him, but there is the sense of being associated with Him in what He is doing and in all His thoughts, so that we are enabled where we are placed to contribute spirituality, sweetness and joy—“Thou shalt glorify me”.

Well, these thoughts are put forward feebly, dear brethren, but I think there is much in them in order that we might the better be able to add to the prosperity of the divine system as we know it here. May the Lord bless the word for His name’s sake.

I would like to say something as to the sons of the prophets. They must have a father somewhere. We all must have a father somewhere. I am thinking of it not just naturally, although we respect our fathers, but in this second book of Kings there is quite a lot about the sons of the prophets who were claiming the fathers and the prophets.
We listen to ministry and all nod in assent as

if we are all agreeing with everything said, but afterwards the question is, How much of it is mine, my own? Here you find this company of the sons of the prophets. We are not to despise the prophets, but these are the sons of the prophets. Have they reached what the prophets were at? We come to a ministry meeting or a reading meeting and the Lord gives something of a prophetic character to touch us, and we may fail to get it. The Lord is yearning for us to come into blessing. That is in His mind all the time; He wants us to come into His thoughts.

In the second chapter the sons of the prophets thought they knew so much. They said, ‘Do you know what is happening today?’ They were up-to-date in everything, and Elisha said, ‘I know it’. But later on, when God takes up Elijah by a whirlwind and when Elisha returns across Jordan with the double portion of Elijah’s spirit, the sons of the prophets were found out; they were in doubt; they did not believe. We find it in ourselves. While we assent in one way, on the other hand we may miss the point.

I read this portion because there is something right about the desire here. The sons of the prophets are sometimes right, sometimes wrong, and here they seemed right in their desire to go to the Jordan. It is safe enough to go to the Jordan. Acquaint yourself with the Jordan!

Acquaint yourself with the death of Christ! The Red Sea is one thing: what He has done for us; and then the Jordan is our death with Him. Acquaint yourself with that! That is the point here. Elisha seems to approve when they say “the place ... is too strait for us”. There is plenty of room to expand at the Jordan. Paul says, “Let your heart also expand itself” (2 Corinthians 6: 13), and in this area there is room for expansion. We were thinking about certain things that middle-aged men are in danger of. I know from experience what it is to
desire to expand in a way that is of no value to me. Expand in this area, near the Jordan, near Gilgal; you can safely expand there! Acquaint yourself with death with Christ.

What goes on here exposes one of the sons of the prophets, but there is something honest about him. We have often hit him and, as long as you apply it to yourself, you can hit as hard as you like! He was felling a beam and he had an axe, and he was left with the handle and the axe-head was in the water. He says, “Alas, master, and it was borrowed!” We may nod our heads while the meeting goes on, but we may afterwards discover that so much is borrowed!

What this brings out here is that we do not need to be down-hearted by it. I look round on these brothers and sisters here and I know they have borrowed quite a lot; many things they have are just borrowed. I quote ministry, and I can quote the ministry as if it were mine. I say,
‘Well, Mr. Taylor said it’. Yes, it is safe enough that he said it, but it does not mean that I have got it—“Alas ... and it was borrowed!”

What does the man of God do here? Does he say, ‘Well, that is you sacked; we can cut you out’? No, he does not say that, he says, “Where did it fall?” That is the point. He was honest enough; he says, ‘Just down there’. I got it at meetings and I thought it was mine and I had not got it at all. It says of Elisha, “And he cut down a stick”. He cuts you down to size, just your own size. In Exodus 15 Jehovah showed Moses wood. Here he gets a stick, not a beam but a stick. Another order of manhood is before the man of God here. He does not go for borrowed axes or borrowed chisels, or anything else. He cuts it down himself. “And the man of God said, Where did it fall? And he shewed him the place. And he cut down a stick, and cast it in thither, and made the iron to swim”.

It is an amazing thing that where naturally everything else goes down, something is made to swim. It is not just a question of floating; you may be just floating; it is not that. He causes it to swim. As a result he says, “Take it up to thee”. I think that is what the Lord is saying to us—‘Take it to yourself’. The message for us is to become engaged with the things that have been before us and not to lose them. The enemy would be active to occupy us with other things, but what has been before us the Holy Spirit would help us to engage in all the time.

‘All things of Jesus’ He knows (hymn 412), and He would like us to be engaged in them all the time. I think that is what happens here. He says, Take it up to thee. “And he put out his hand and took it”. Let us take it, for His name’s sake.

text: Darby *
To walk with God! O fellowship divine!
Man’s highest state on earth—Lord be it mine!
With Thee may I a close communion hold,
To Thee the deep recesses of my heart unfold—
Yes, tell Thee all, each weary care and grief
Into Thy bosom pour, till there I find relief,
Oh let me walk with Thee, Thou mighty One,
Lean on Thine arm and trust Thy love alone.
With Thee hold converse sweet where’er I go,
Thy smile of love my highest bliss below,
With Thee transact life’s business, doing all
With single aim for Thee as Thou dost call,
My every comfort at Thy hand receive.
My every talent to Thy glory give.
Thy counsel seek in every trying hour,
In all my weakness trust Thy mighty power.
Oh may this high companionship be mine
And all my life by its reflection shine!
My great, my wise, my never-failing Friend!
Whose life no change can know, no turn, no end.
My Saviour-God who gav’st Thy life for me,
Let nothing come between my heart and Thee!
From Thee no thought, no secret would I keep
But on Thy breast my tears of anguish weep.
My every wound I take to Thee to heal
For Thou art touched by every pang I feel,
In Thee and Thee alone I now confide,
And Thee I’d follow as my Lord and Guide.
Earth’s broken cisterns ah! they all have proved
Unsatisfying, vain, however loved!
The false must fail, the fondest they must go!
Oh thus it is with all we love below!
From things of earth then let my heart be free
And find its happiness, my Lord, in Thee,
The Holy Spirit for my Guide and Guest,
Whate’er my lot, I must be safe and blest.
Washed in Thy blood, from all my guilt made clean,
I in Thy righteousness alone am seen;
Thy home, my home, Thy God and Father mine,
Dead to the world, my life is hid in Thine;
Its highest honours fade before my view,
Its pleasures—I can trample on them too.
With Thee by faith I walk in crowds alone,
Making to Thee my wants and wishes known,
Drawing from Thee my daily strength in prayer,
Finding Thine arm sustains me everywhere,
While through the clouds of sin and woe the light
Of coming glory shines more sweetly bright,
And This my daily boast, my aim, my end,
That my Redeemer is my God, my Friend.
This poem, attributed to Mr. Darby, was found recently among second-hand books in a Malvern shop. Its character and quality would indicate that he was, in fact, the author. It seems that in copying
the verses a line has been omitted near the end—Ed. (see No. 91 June p.22)

paragraphs.text: START COLLECTING! Many younger readers will be collectors, maybe of books, flowers, shells, or rocks. Most of us have collected postage stamps at some time in our lives. Some keep a record of the different kinds of birds they have observed. Now Solomon, to whom God gave outstanding wisdom, has some advice for us on collecting. He says, “The words of the wise are as goads, and the collections of them (the footnote says it may read, ‘those who collect them’) as nails fastened in: they are given from one shepherd”, Ecclesiastes 12: 11.
One of the best things any of us can do is to start a collection of “the words of the wise”.

These words come to us as we read the Scriptures and ministry, and in our meetings, and they are very precious because they are given to us by our great Shepherd. So let us treasure the impressions He gives us and go over them in prayer and exercise, so that they are “fastened in”, like nails, and become part of us. It is often helpful, I find, to write down impressions—
that helps to get them fastened in.

Why are the words spoken of as ‘goads’? A goad was a pointed pole used to poke oxen to keep them on the move or make them move faster. So the words we receive will often prick the conscience, especially if we are getting a bit slack. How thankful we should be for the faithful love of Christ who sends his word so that we are kept moving on in the path of His will, which is the way of happiness and blessing.
